title: Caché - San Francisco
text: Design and development of French bistro in San Francisco.
label: Discover

details.box:
Overview

Timeline:

November 2024 - January 2025

Role:

Product Design (UX/UI) - Web Developer

Tools:

Figma, WordPress, HTML, CSS
details.txt:
Background & Challenge

Caché is a modern neighborhood bistro in San Francisco that blends a relaxed French bistro atmosphere with contemporary culinary experiences. The restaurant needed a digital presence that reflected its identity, provided essential information, and facilitated reservations while optimizing for both desktop and mobile users.

The challenge was to create a website that not only showcased the brand's unique personality but also delivered a seamless user experience for customers seeking details about the menu, reservations, and events.

Understanding the Audience

Before opening Figma, I sat down with the owners to walk through a typical week at the restaurant: who books ahead, who walks in, who comes back. That conversation, combined with a look at comparable San Francisco bistro sites, shaped three audience groups I designed around:

  1. Local Residents & Tourists : Seeking an elevated but welcoming dining experience, usually deciding same-day or same-week.
  2. Food Enthusiasts & Millennials : Interested in modern gastronomy and natural wines, more likely to check the menu and Instagram before booking.
  3. Casual & Special Occasion Diners : Exploring options for brunch, happy hour, or dinner, often comparing a handful of restaurants before committing.

The common thread across all three was that people wanted to see the menu and make a reservation within a couple of taps, without digging through a cluttered homepage. That became the north star for the layout: menu and booking always one click away, never buried under marketing copy.

details.title: Design Approach & Strategy
lines: The design focused on elegance and warmth, capturing the bistro's inviting yet sophisticated atmosphere. Key elements included:

1. Color Palette

    2. I selected a terra cotta shade (#B86C51) that evokes warmth and a natural feel, complemented by an off-white background (#FBEBD9) to create a clean and airy aesthetic.

1. Custom Logo Design

    2. Instead of using an existing font, I hand-wrote the restaurant's name on paper, scanned it, and vectorized it to create a unique and personal brand identity. This gave the logo a handcrafted, distinctive feel.

details.txt:
1. Typography
    2. The main text fonts are Ruffina for its refined and expressive character, paired with Lato for a modern and highly readable contrast.
  2. Icons & Visual Accents
    3. I designed additional custom icons, including an Instagram logo, a fish, and a carrot, allowing flexibility for the client to add visual markers for social media, seafood, or vegetarian dishes.

Development & Implementation

Using WordPress as the CMS allowed for flexible content management while ensuring smooth performance. Custom HTML and CSS were incorporated to refine styling beyond standard templates, ensuring brand consistency. Specific optimizations included:
  • A fully responsive menu and booking system
  • Fast-loading pages with optimized media content
  • SEO best practices to enhance discoverability

away.title: Take-aways
away.text: The site launched with the menu and reservation flow front and center, which is exactly what the owners had asked for after seeing how many of their regulars were booking from their phones. Building the logo from a scanned, hand-written mark instead of a stock font turned out to be the detail people mentioned most, it gave the brand a handmade feel that matched the food. Working inside WordPress also meant the owners could update the menu themselves once I handed the site off, which mattered more to them long-term than any single design decision I made. If I revisited this project, I'd push for a short round of user testing with real diners before launch rather than relying on my own walkthroughs, since a couple of the reservation-flow tweaks I made post-launch would have surfaced earlier.

title: The Collectible
text: Co-founded and built an art marketplace mobile app — Flutter/Dart on GCP/Firebase.
label: Read More

details.box:
Overview

Timeline:

January 2023 - August 2024

Role:

Co-Founder, CTO & Product Designer

Tools:

Figma, Flutter, Dart, Firebase, GCP
details.txt:
Context

TheCollectible is an entrepreneurial initiative I co-founded to create a user-friendly marketplace for art and collectibles. As CTO, I led the technical direction while actively contributing to UX research and product design. The core problem we set out to solve was trust: collectors couldn't evaluate condition, provenance, or authenticity from a standard listing, and they had no one to ask.

Research identified key pain points: difficulty accessing art, evaluating collectibles, and navigating existing platforms. Users needed a trustworthy, intuitive marketplace with seamless transactions and curated content.

Audience & Research

I started with interviews with people who collect art or one-off pieces, plus a short survey shared in collector communities. The recurring frustration was trust: people didn't know how to judge condition or authenticity from a listing. That shaped two personas:

  • The Careful Collector — disposable income, wants provenance and detail before spending, will not rush.
  • The Casual Browser — drawn in by a specific piece, needs the buying process explained in plain language.

From there I mapped the user flow around a single goal: get a browser from a listing they like to a confident purchase without needing to message anyone first. Provenance and condition details moved up next to the price — before any high-fidelity work started — which was the single biggest structural change to come out of this research stage.

Product Design & Brand

The brand needed to feel more like a gallery than a marketplace. I leaned into a darker, editorial palette with a serif wordmark instead of the bright, high-contrast look most marketplace apps use. I built a small design system — type scale, spacing tokens, component states — early on so the web and mobile builds wouldn't drift apart as the team grew.

Low-fidelity wireframes settled the listing page layout first, since that's where the trust problem lived. I then built high-fidelity prototypes in Figma and walked a handful of collectors through them before any code was written.

Technical Architecture

The platform was built in Flutter/Dart for a shared codebase across web and mobile, on top of a Firebase backend for auth, listings, and storage on GCP. As CTO I made the call to keep the stack small and boring on purpose — we were a small team and I didn't want to be debugging infrastructure instead of shipping the listing flow.

We launched with a small, invite-based seller pool so I could watch how real listings performed before opening things up. That let me catch edge cases in the listing form (multiple images, pricing in different currencies) before they became support tickets. As Scrum Master I coordinated delivery across engineering and product, communicating priorities and risk to both technical and non-technical partners.
details.alt: TheCollectible brand identity and design system

details.title: The Development Process
details.subtitle: The process followed a structured UX and engineering approach:
lines: • User Research & Strategy
Interviews and surveys with collectors shaped two key personas and a north-star user flow: from discovery to confident purchase without needing to message anyone first.
• Branding & Visual Identity
Dark editorial palette, serif wordmark, and a design system (type scale, spacing, component states) built early to keep web and mobile consistent as the team grew.
• Wireframing & Prototyping

Low-fidelity wireframes settled the listing page structure. Provenance and condition moved next to price before any high-fidelity work started — the single biggest change from research. High-fidelity Figma prototypes were tested with real collectors before code was written.
• Technical Development
Flutter/Dart shared codebase for web and mobile; Firebase for auth, listings, and storage on GCP. Small, stable stack kept the team focused on shipping the listing flow rather than infrastructure.
• Testing & Refinement

Listing flow and search changed the most after early feedback. Filtering by medium and price range was added earlier than planned once it became clear users arrived with a specific piece in mind, not browsing everything.
• Deployment & Scaling
Invite-based seller launch caught edge cases in the listing form (multiple images, multi-currency pricing) before they became support tickets.

away.title: Takeaways
text: The biggest lesson from TheCollectible wasn't a design pattern, it was how much of the UX work turned out to be about trust rather than layout. Once I understood that collectors needed proof and context before they'd buy, most of the interface decisions followed naturally.

Wearing both the CTO and design hats also taught me to pick fights carefully: I said no to a few feature ideas that would have looked good in a pitch deck but would have slowed down the one flow that actually mattered — getting from a listing to a confident purchase.

title: Divorce.fm
text: Development of an online radio with a self-managed CMS.
label: Read More

details.box:
Overview

Timeline:

January 2024 - August 2024

Role:

Web Developer

Tools:

PHP, Laravel, MySQL, Tailwind CSS, Alpine.js, SoundCloud API
details.txt:
Background & Challenge

The client wanted an online radio built around SoundCloud mixes, with a deliberately old-school, slightly chaotic feel: random backgrounds, a hue-shifting logo, playful button art. The visual direction and branding came from my partner — my job was turning that into a real site the client could run day to day.

The brief also included self-management: the client needed to add new mixes and swap background images without calling me every time. That made the real engineering problem the admin panel, not the player.

The Radio Player

The public-facing side is plain JavaScript wrapped around the SoundCloud widget: play, pause, skip, and a volume control that occasionally lands on a joke value instead of a real percentage — the client wanted the whole thing to feel a bit unserious. The logo and buttons get a random hue shift on load, and long track titles scroll like a vintage marquee instead of being cut off.

Ads are skipped on mobile on purpose: autoplaying a sponsor track over mobile data felt like the wrong default. The palette stayed deliberately minimal — black and white with a single accent color — so the background images the client uploads stay the focal point.

details.title: Two Versions, One Site
lines: The first version shipped in July 2024: a plain PHP and MySQL site running on Apache, built fast to get the client something real to test and use. Once it was clear the admin side needed to do more than a login form and a few uploads, I rebuilt the backend in Laravel over the following months, with Breeze handling authentication and a proper admin panel replacing the hand-rolled one.

details.txt:
The Admin Panel

Once rebuilt in Laravel, the admin panel became the core of the product. The client pastes a raw SoundCloud link and the app parses artist and title straight out of the URL — no manual data entry. A separate pool of sponsor tracks plays between mixes, chosen by whichever has been played least, so no single ad gets overplayed.

Background images can be uploaded one at a time or dropped as a folder — the app syncs them into the database and resizes and compresses each one automatically, including animated GIFs. If the database connection drops, the site falls back to a maintenance page instead of crashing. A radio going down felt worse than most sites going down.

details.title: What the Admin Panel Actually Does
details.subtitle: Once rebuilt in Laravel, the panel handled:
lines: • Track management
The admin pastes a raw SoundCloud link and the app parses the artist and title straight out of the URL, no manual data entry.
• Ad rotation
A separate pool of sponsor tracks plays between mixes, chosen by whichever has been played the least, so no single ad gets overplayed.
• Background management
The client uploads images directly, or drops a folder of files and the app syncs them into the database. Every image gets resized and compressed automatically, including animated GIFs.
• Fallback handling
If the database connection drops, the site falls back to a maintenance page instead of crashing. A radio station going down felt worse than most sites going down.

details.txt:
Color & Visual Identity

The palette stayed deliberately minimal — black and white with a single accent color — so the background images the client uploads stay the focal point instead of competing with the UI. The accent color shifts hue on every page load, giving each visit a slightly different feel without changing the structure.

away.title: Takeaways
text: This project taught me when to rebuild instead of patch. The first PHP version got the client live fast, but once the admin requirements grew past a login form and a few uploads, hand-rolling that in plain PHP would have meant reinventing a framework badly. Moving to Laravel for the second version gave the client a panel that actually holds up: real authentication, validated uploads, and image processing that doesn't need me on call every time they want to add a background.
It's also the project where I got comfortable telling a client that a feature belongs behind a real framework instead of stacking more custom PHP on top of what was already there.
